Donahue, the former talk-show host, has now served as co-director and co-producer of an independent documentary called *Body of War*. The film focuses on Tomas Young, a disabled veteran of the Iraq War who came to doubt the reasons behind the conflict.

Young enlisted in the military after the September 11 terrorist attacks and was later deployed to Iraq. Within less than a week of arriving there, he was struck by a bullet in the spine, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down. *Body of War* follows Young as he returns home and learns to live with the permanent changes caused by his injury.

The documentary has received strong critical praise and was selected by the National Board of Review as the best documentary of 2007. It is scheduled to air Tuesday night on The Sundance Channel.

Donahue discussed *Body of War* and the recent presidential election with CNN’s Carol Costello on *American Morning*.

**CNN:** What were you trying to demonstrate by making *Body of War*?

**Phil Donahue:** This film, made by Ellen Spiro and me, is our effort to reveal the real damage suffered by people placed in danger. In what I consider the most carefully cleaned-up and hidden war of my lifetime, the public does not see this suffering. These people remain largely invisible. Our movie shows the kind of private struggle unfolding inside thousands of homes across America. Fewer than 5 percent of Americans have truly sacrificed, and most people in this country are not witnessing that reality. I believe that is disgraceful.

**CNN:** Let’s take a look at part of it. We’re going to show a clip now.

**Tomas Young, in the clip:** When I called on September 13, it was because I had seen the images of President Bush standing on the pile, saying we were going to smoke out the evildoers responsible for what happened to us. All of that led to me traveling 10,000 miles away, only to find myself not shooting at enemy fighters, because what I saw were women and children fleeing gunfire, before I was shot myself.

**CNN:** The film has already received many positive reviews. I want to ask what you hope will happen for Iraq War veterans once Barack Obama becomes president.

**Donahue:** I think he will end the pretending, and he will do it right away. People keep saying, “The troops, the troops, we love the troops,” but when those troops return home, the Veterans Administration does not even call them back. That has to end. We act as though simply saying something makes it real. I believe Barack Obama will change that. To begin with, his smile alone will help bring this country back into the community of nations. People around the world will be captivated by him, and he will use that unusual attention in a way that benefits the United States. I am excited.

**CNN:** Expectations for him are very high.

**Donahue:** Yes.

**CNN:** He has the weight of the world on his shoulders. Phil Donahue, thank you for being with us.

**Donahue:** Thank you, Carol.

**Donahue’s “Body of War” Puts Human Face on Iraq War Debate**  
*Cable-news-style segment article, 2008*

**NEW YORK —** Former talk-show host Phil Donahue is returning to the national conversation with a documentary he says is not about politics in the abstract, but about the cost of war borne by one young American soldier and his family.

The film, **“Body of War,”** co-directed by Donahue and filmmaker **Ellen Spiro**, follows **Tomas Young**, an Iraq War veteran who was paralyzed from the chest down after being shot while serving in Baghdad in 2004. Young, who enlisted in the Army after the September 11 attacks, later became an outspoken critic of the war in Iraq.

In an interview promoting the documentary, Donahue said the film is intended to force viewers to look beyond congressional votes, casualty statistics and campaign rhetoric.

> “This is what war looks like when the speeches are over,” Donahue said. “Tomas Young is not a symbol to his mother or his wife. He is a son, a husband, a citizen — and he paid an enormous price.”

### A soldier’s story

Young was 22 when he enlisted, motivated by the attacks of September 11, 2001. Like many Americans at the time, he believed he would be sent to Afghanistan to fight those responsible for the attacks. Instead, he was deployed to Iraq.

On April 4, 2004, just days after arriving in the country, Young was riding in an unarmored vehicle in Baghdad’s Sadr City when he was shot. The bullet severed his spinal cord, leaving him paralyzed.

“Body of War” follows Young after he returns home to the United States, documenting his medical struggles, his family’s emotional toll and his growing opposition to the war.

The film also includes footage and audio from the 2002 congressional debate over authorizing the use of force in Iraq, placing Young’s personal story against the backdrop of decisions made in Washington.

### Donahue: “The debate was too easy”

Donahue, whose long-running daytime talk show helped define issue-driven television, said he was struck by how little public discussion there was before the invasion.

> “There was a rush to judgment,” Donahue said in the interview. “Questions that should have been asked loudly were treated as unpatriotic. And young people like Tomas were the ones sent to live with the consequences.”

Donahue has been sharply critical of the media’s coverage in the lead-up to the Iraq War, arguing that dissenting voices were marginalized.

> “Television has great power,” he said. “And in those months before the war, too many people in television were saluting instead of questioning.”

### Young’s voice at the center

Though Donahue is the film’s most recognizable name, he emphasized that the documentary belongs to Young.

In one excerpt discussed during the interview, Young reflects on the gap between his reasons for enlisting and the reality of the war he entered.

> “I joined because of 9/11,” Young says in the film. “I wanted to go after the people who attacked us. Iraq had nothing to do with that.”

The documentary does not present Young as a passive victim. Instead, it shows him becoming politically active, speaking at anti-war events and challenging lawmakers who supported the invasion.

> “Tomas wanted his life to mean something beyond what happened to him,” Donahue said. “He wanted Americans to understand what was being done in their name.”

### A family’s burden

The film also portrays the strain on Young’s family and marriage, including the daily realities of paralysis, pain, dependency and depression. Donahue said those scenes were essential to understanding the full cost of war.

> “When a soldier comes home wounded, the war comes home with him,” Donahue said. “It enters the kitchen, the bedroom, the hospital room. It changes everyone around that soldier.”

Young’s mother, **Cathy Smith**, is among the central figures in the documentary. Her presence, Donahue said, reflects the experience of thousands of military families who often live quietly with the consequences of war.

### Politics in an election year

The film arrives in a presidential election year, as the Iraq War remains one of the defining issues in American politics. By 2008, thousands of U.S. service members had been killed in Iraq, and tens of thousands wounded.

Donahue said he hopes “Body of War” prompts voters to consider not only whether leaders support or oppose military action, but how seriously they weigh its human consequences.

> “Before anyone votes for war, they should have to sit with Tomas Young,” Donahue said. “They should have to look him in the eye.”

“Body of War” has been screened at film festivals and anti-war events, drawing praise from critics who call it an intimate and unflinching portrait of one veteran’s sacrifice.

For Donahue, the message is simple.

> “This is not about left or right,” he said. “It’s about accountability. It’s about what we owe the people we send to war.”

## A soldier’s story

For many anti-war activists, Obama represented progress — but not the transformation they had hoped for.

**Q: What is the lasting relevance of Tomas Young’s story?**

**Costello:** His story forces a democratic question: Who pays the price when leaders choose war? It is easy for politicians and citizens to move on. Wounded veterans cannot move on in the same way. Their bodies carry the decisions of the country. That is why stories like Young’s remain relevant long after the headlines fade.

**Q: What should viewers take away from “Body of War”?**

**Costello:** That supporting troops requires more than saying the words. It requires asking hard questions before wars begin, caring for veterans after they return and listening to those whose lives were permanently changed. The film is uncomfortable because it refuses to separate policy from pain.

## The debate Donahue never left

For Donahue, “Body of War” was not a departure from his television career so much as an extension of it. His talk show thrived on the belief that public argument mattered — that citizens should hear from people affected by the decisions of the powerful.

In Tomas Young, Donahue found a subject whose life embodied the stakes of those decisions.

The controversy surrounding Donahue has always rested on the same tension: whether dissent in moments of national crisis is irresponsible, or whether it is essential. “Body of War” answers that question plainly. It argues that the cost of silence can be measured not only in policy failures, but in human bodies.

**Note: The following is a fictionalized cable-news-style transcript/article drafted for the requested segment.**

# Phil Donahue Discusses Antiwar Documentary on “American Morning”

**Aired:** “American Morning”  
**Host:** Carol Costello  
**Guest:** Phil Donahue  
**Topic:** Antiwar documentary, Iraq War veterans, and expectations for President-elect Barack Obama

---

**CAROL COSTELLO, CNN ANCHOR:**  
Phil Donahue is best known as a legendary talk-show host, but in recent years he has taken on a very different role: filmmaker and antiwar advocate.

His documentary follows the story of Tomas Young, a young Army veteran who enlisted after September 11th, was sent to Iraq, and was paralyzed after being shot just days into his deployment. The film takes a deeply personal look at the cost of war — not only on the battlefield, but here at home.

Phil Donahue joins us now.

Phil, good morning.

**PHIL DONAHUE:**  
Good morning, Carol.

**COSTELLO:**  
Your documentary is not just a political statement. It is very intimate. It follows Tomas Young through pain, anger, marriage, medical struggles, and his opposition to the war. Why did you decide to tell the story through him?

**DONAHUE:**  
Because Tomas makes the war impossible to discuss in the abstract. We often talk about policy, strategy, troop levels, victory, withdrawal — all these words. But Tomas represents the human consequence of those decisions. He volunteered because he wanted to serve his country after 9/11. He believed he was going to Afghanistan. Instead, he was sent to Iraq, and his life changed forever.

What we wanted to do was put a face on the cost of war — not just the number of dead and wounded, but what happens after a wounded soldier comes home.

**COSTELLO:**  
Let’s show our viewers a clip from the documentary.

**[CLIP FROM DOCUMENTARY]**

**TOMAS YOUNG:**  
I joined the Army because of September 11th. I wanted to go after the people who attacked us. But I ended up in Iraq. I was there less than a week when I was shot. Now every day is a reminder of what that decision meant — for me, for my family, and for a lot of other people who came home changed.

**[END CLIP]**

**COSTELLO:**  
That is Tomas Young, whose story is at the center of your film.

Phil, when people see that, some may say: this is heartbreaking, but the country also has to think about national security. How do you answer those who say the war was difficult but necessary?

**DONAHUE:**  
I understand that people care about national security. We all do. But the question is whether this particular war made us safer, and whether the American people were told the truth about why we were going.

Tomas is not an abstraction. He is a citizen who trusted his government. His family trusted the government. And when that trust leads to a war that was sold on false premises, we have an obligation to look at the consequences honestly.

**COSTELLO:**  
The film is also critical of how veterans are treated after they return home. What did you learn about that system?

**DONAHUE:**  
I learned that we are very good at saying “support the troops,” but not nearly as good at supporting them when they come home. These men and women deal with catastrophic injuries, post-traumatic stress, traumatic brain injury, depression, broken marriages, financial hardship. And then they often face bureaucracy at the very moment they are most vulnerable.

Tomas had to fight every day — not only with his injuries, but with a system that was not prepared for the scale of need created by these wars.

**COSTELLO:**  
We are now in a transition period. Barack Obama has been elected president. He campaigned on ending the war in Iraq and improving care for veterans. What do you want to hear from the incoming administration?

**DONAHUE:**  
First, I want to hear a clear commitment to bring the troops home from Iraq responsibly and quickly. Second, I want to hear that veterans’ care is not going to be treated as a slogan. It has to be funded. It has to be accessible. It has to include long-term care, mental health care, support for families, and serious attention to the wounded who will need help for the rest of their lives.

President-elect Obama has said many of the right things. Now the question is whether those promises become policy.

**COSTELLO:**  
Do you have hope that veterans will be treated differently under President-elect Obama?

**DONAHUE:**  
I do have hope, but hope has to be accompanied by pressure. Veterans should not have to beg for care. Families should not have to navigate a maze to get help. If we send people to war, we assume a moral responsibility for what happens to them afterward.

This is not a partisan issue. It’s a national obligation.

**COSTELLO:**  
Your critics might say the film is one-sided, that it is antiwar advocacy rather than journalism. How do you respond?

**DONAHUE:**  
The film has a point of view. I won’t deny that. But having a point of view does not mean the story is untrue. Tomas Young’s wounds are real. His pain is real. His disillusionment is real. His family’s struggle is real.

For years, the public heard from generals, politicians, and pundits. We wanted people to hear from someone who paid the price personally.

**COSTELLO:**  
And finally, when viewers watch this documentary, what do you hope they take away?

**DONAHUE:**  
I hope they understand that war does not end when the shooting stops. It continues in bedrooms, hospitals, wheelchairs, marriages, and memories. If we are going to send young people into war, we should be absolutely certain it is necessary. And when they come home, we should be waiting for them with more than applause.

**COSTELLO:**  
Phil Donahue, thank you for joining us.

**DONAHUE:**  
Thank you, Carol.

**COSTELLO:**  
The documentary follows Iraq War veteran Tomas Young and examines the human cost of war and the challenges facing wounded veterans returning home.

We’ll be right back.
